characters: Dzigbodi: an expressive seven-year-old Ghanaian girl with neat cornrows and yellow hair ribbons, wearing a sunny coral-and-cream house dress.
Mama: her calm, loving Ghanaian mother wearing a turquoise-and-gold African-print wrapper cloth and matching headscarf.

narrationPlan.voice: A small, worried voice for Dzigbodi; a calm, loving voice for Mama
narrationPlan.pace: Soft and slow at the hiding, brighter after the truth (about 90 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: A tense, quiet tune that turns warm after the truth (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Honesty and owning up promptly are deeply valued across Ghanaian homes and classrooms.
The story models calm, restorative parenting—pairing warmth with responsible repair—while emphasizing that adults, never young children, pick up sharp broken ceramic or glass.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Confirm that broken-pottery safety (children step back and fetch an adult rather than touching shards) is unmistakable.
Confirm that the tone stays empathetic toward children who feel anxious when owning up.

teacherGuide.overview: A relatable character-education story about owning up to an indoor accident, contrasting the heavy feeling of secrecy with the relief of honesty, restorative action, and safety around broken crockery.
learningGoals: Describe how hiding a mistake feels compared with telling the truth.
Explain why honesty protects trust between people.
State the safety rule when glass or china breaks (never touch sharp pieces; tell an adult).
beforeReading: Ask: have you ever knocked something over by accident? How did your body feel in that first moment?
whileReading: Pause on page 3 and ask: what brave choice can Dzigbodi make right now?
afterReading: Practise a polite, honest apology in pairs: “I am sorry that I ___. How can I help put it right?”
Complete the sentence: “When something breaks, I stay safe by ___.”
discussion: Why did Dzigbodi’s tummy ache while she hid the broken cup?
Why did Mama ask Dzigbodi to stand back while Mama picked up the sharp pieces?
reflection: Who is a trusted grown-up you can go to whenever you make a mistake?

support: Match four facial-expression cards (startled, worried, tearful, relieved) to pages 1, 2, 4, and 6.
stretch: Write three sentences showing what Dzigbodi says to a younger cousin who wants to kick a ball indoors the next week.

culturalNotes: Honesty and owning up promptly are deeply valued across Ghanaian homes and classrooms.
The story models calm, restorative parenting—pairing warmth with responsible repair—while emphasizing that adults, never young children, pick up sharp broken ceramic or glass.
localiseThis: Practise respectful expressions for apologizing in learners’ home languages as well as English.
Respond gently in class whenever pupils own up to honest accidents so honesty feels safe.
